abstract:
Emerging spatial multi-omics technologies enable the simultaneous profiling of multiple molecular layers within the same tissue section, offering new opportunities to interrogate tissue organization in its native spatial context. However, sequencing-derived spatial multi-omics data are often affected by intrinsic perturbations, such as technical noise, missing values, sparsity and measurement bias. These perturbations make existing methods that mainly use spatial graphs for neighborhood aggregation insufficient to recover continuous tissue-region structures, while unconstrained representation learning may propagate noisy associations and lead to fragmented spatial domains.
We present SpatialMuSC, a robust spatial multi-omics integration framework centering on spatial graph-conditioned diffusion refinement and perturbation-invariant fusion consistency. SpatialMuSC introduces spatial topology as conditional information into the latent diffusion process, enabling spatial adjacency to guide neighborhood aggregation, spatial structure propagation and graph-aware denoising of latent states. Perturbation-invariant fusion consistency further encourages stable multi-omic fusion under perturbed observations. We evaluate SpatialMuSC on diverse spatial multi-omics datasets across different tissues and sequencing platforms, including 10x Visium, Stereo-CITE-seq, SPOTS and spatial epigenome-transcriptome data. Across these benchmarks, SpatialMuSC consistently outperforms ten state-of-the-art methods in spatial domain identification and tissue-structure preservation. Ablation analyses confirm the contributions of graph-conditioned diffusion refinement and perturbation-invariant fusion consistency, rather than post hoc graph smoothing or graph propagation alone. In particular, SpatialMuSC effectively distinguishes adjacent tissue regions, preserves block-wise smoothness and layered architectures, and shows more stable performance in missing-observation stress tests, while hippocampal marker, enrichment, and paired RNA-ATAC analyses identify a GCL-associated neuronal program and a TTR-associated accessibility feature in a choroid plexus-enriched domain.
The source code is available at https://github.com/CSUBioGroup/SpatialMuSC.
Supplementary data are available online.
